evidence.note: URAA (17 USC 104A) restores foreign works that entered US public domain via formality failure (e.g., non-renewal), not works whose full statutory term naturally ran out. If the 1921 US release 'I Accuse' was renewed, the 56-year term expired by 1977, before URAA's reference date, so restoration is unavailable regardless of France's continuing copyright (Gance, d. 1981; French term through 2051). If it was never renewed, a URAA concern remains open; the renewal_search DIY links provide the means to resolve it. The queue classification 'renewal_truth: term_expiry' reflects prior research supporting the term-expiry path.
evidence.source: 17 USC 104A â€” URAA copyright restoration provisions

editorial:
Abel Gance's J'accuse! (1919) was shot in part on active WWI battlefields â€” Charles PathÃ© secured French Army cooperation, and Gance recruited several thousand soldiers as extras for the climactic sequence of the dead rising from their graves; many of those men died in the Verdun offensive within weeks of filming. Produced by PathÃ© FrÃ¨res and released in France in April 1919, it arrived in the US in 1921 under the title 'I Accuse' in an edited version distributed by United Artists, with the universalist anti-war message softened and a happier ending grafted on for American audiences. The imagery Gance created â€” gaunt corpses confronting the living with the question of whether their deaths meant anything â€” has since become one of silent cinema's most cited visual inheritances.

The practical rights trap for any reuser is not the 1919 film itself but the 2008 Flicker Alley restoration. Lobster Films (Paris) spent years assembling footage from the Czech Film Archive, the CinÃ©mathÃ¨que FranÃ§aise, and the Nederlands Filmmuseum to reconstruct the most complete edition since the original release, and Flicker Alley issued it on DVD with a newly commissioned score. That restoration and its score carry independent copyright; a filmmaker who rips the Flicker Alley disc or streams from a service that licensed it is using a protected editorial compilation, not the bare 1919 images. Clean access to the underlying photographic images requires sourcing an unrestored print through a national film archive and, if music is needed, commissioning original music.
faq: Can I use J'accuse! footage in my film or documentary?

The 1919 photographic images are in the US public domain â€” the film predates the pre-1930 term-expiry boundary and no copyright on the images remains. The obstacle is sourcing: the most widely available version is the 2008 Flicker Alley / Lobster Films restoration, and that release's editorial compilation and newly composed score are separately protected. To use the footage without complication, obtain an unrestored archival print from a national film archive (Library of Congress, CinÃ©mathÃ¨que FranÃ§aise, or Nederlands Filmmuseum) rather than deriving from any commercial edition.
Does the URAA affect J'accuse! the way it does some other French silent films?

Possibly, but the term-expiry path likely forecloses it. URAA restores foreign works that entered US public domain through a formality failure â€” such as non-renewal â€” when the source country's copyright was still alive on January 1 1996. Abel Gance's heirs hold French rights until 2051, so that condition is met. Whether URAA actually applies turns on whether the 1921 US release 'I Accuse' was ever renewed: if it was renewed, the full 56-year term expired by 1977, which is before URAA's reference date, and there is nothing for URAA to restore; if it was never renewed, URAA potentially applies. Run the Stanford Copyright Renewal Database search for 'I Accuse' in the 1948â€“1950 range to close this question before relying on the film in a high-stakes commercial context.
